newsitem.title: USA: U.S. defense chief says more base closures needed.
newsitem.headline: U.S. defense chief says more base closures needed.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen said on Monday he was disappointed that Congress had postponed a new round of military base reductions and said more base closures were needed.

"We still need to go through more base closure processes," Cohen told local officials and business leaders during a visit to the former Naval Air Station Alameda, a recently closed military base on San Francisco Bay that is being converted to civilian use.
Cohen noted that his proposal for two new rounds of military base closures in 1999 and 2001 had "not been greeted with overwhelming enthusiasm by the U.S. Congress."

He suggested that the former Alameda base, now home to a number of private businesses, could be held up as a model to members of Congress who were concerned that closing military bases in their areas would lead to a loss of jobs.

"I'm more persuaded than ever that if the people of this country can see what is taking place here -- if we can make it a complete success -- it will in fact provide the role model for other communities," he told reporters.

The Senate voted earlier this month to delay the next round of base closures until early in 2001, pending further analysis by the Pentagon and government economists of how much the closures actually save.
The version of the defence bill passed by the House omitted the authorisation of base closings.
Cohen said he was disappointed but not surprised that Congress decided not to authorise additional rounds of base closures.
He said the United States was in the middle of reducing its force structure by about 36 percent but had reduced its infrastructure by only about 22 percent.

"We have got to come down more if we hope to really deal with our problems," he added. "The problem we are having is that we're not saving enough from our operations to put into research and development for the future."
He said that if Alameda could be taken as an example of what could be done, "then I think that we can have those base closures in the future."
Cohen has previously estimated that the base closures he proposed would save about $2.7 billion a year, which would help pay for billions of dollars in high-tech weaponry for the 21st century.

At the former Alameda base, Cohen toured two private businesses that have been set up in hangars. One makes valves for nuclear submarines and power plants, and another, Calstart, has received Department of Defence funding to develop electric and hybrid electric vehicle technologies.
Cohen had a test drive in an electric car and heard concerns from local officials about toxic cleanup at the former military base and whether the federal government would pay for it.
"We believe that the clean up has to take place and obviously we need to provide the funding for it," Cohen told reporters.
